passages.happening:
The apostles and believers throughout Judea hear that the Gentiles too have received the word of God (verse 1). When Peter goes up to Jerusalem, the circumcised believers take issue with him. “You visited uncircumcised men and ate with them,” they say (verse 3).

Peter does not argue. He tells them the whole story in order (verse 4). He was praying in Joppa and saw the sheet let down from heaven, full of animals, reptiles and birds. He heard a voice: ‘Get up, Peter, kill and eat.’ He answered, ‘No, Lord, for nothing impure or unclean has ever entered my mouth.’ The voice spoke again: “Do not call anything impure that God has made clean” (verse 9). This happened three times, and everything was drawn back up into heaven (verses 5-10).
passages.hearers:
‘The circumcised believers’ are Jewish believers in Jesus, the church in Jerusalem. They are not enemies of the gospel. They are faithful Jews who have believed that Jesus is the Messiah, and they are troubled.

Notice what they complain about. Not that Peter preached to Gentiles, but that he ‘ate with them’. In that world a shared meal meant belonging. To eat at someone's table was to accept him as one of your own. For many devout Jews, eating with Gentiles risked food that broke the Law and blurred the line God had drawn around Israel. Their question is a fair one: can Peter, a Jew and an apostle, simply set that line aside?

Peter's answer is wise. He does not start with an argument. He tells what happened, step by step, and lets the story speak. He even tells them his own first answer, ‘No, Lord’. He admits that he resisted too.

This question did not go away. Years later Paul tells how Peter ate with Gentiles at Antioch, then drew back when ‘certain men came from James’ (Galatians 2:12). Even Peter found this hard to live out.
passages.ot:
The believers' worry comes from the Law. God had told Israel, “I have set you apart from the nations to be My own” (Leviticus 20:26), and the food laws were a daily sign of that. Their concern is not small-minded. It comes from love for what God had said.

But the Scriptures also promised that the nations would come. “All nations will stream to it,” Isaiah said of God's house (Isaiah 2:2), and the peoples would say, “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD” (Isaiah 2:3). The question in Jerusalem is how the two promises fit together.
passages.asks: The Jerusalem believers asked a hard question, and Peter answered with a true story, told humbly, including his own resistance. Ask how you speak when you disagree with other believers. And ask whether you are willing to admit, as Peter did, that you were slow to see what God was doing.

passages.happening:
Peter goes on. Just then three men from Caesarea arrived. The Spirit told him to go with them “without hesitation” (verse 12). Six brothers went with him, and they entered the man's home. The man told them an angel had said, ‘Send to Joppa for Simon who is called Peter. He will convey to you a message by which you and all your household will be saved’ (verses 13-14).

“As I began to speak,” Peter says, “the Holy Spirit fell upon them, just as He had fallen upon us at the beginning” (verse 15). Then he remembered the Lord's words, ‘John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit’ (verse 16). “So if God gave them the same gift He gave us who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I to hinder the work of God?” (verse 17).

The objections stop. They praise God and say, “So then, God has granted even the Gentiles repentance unto life” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Peter points to the six brothers. They are standing there as witnesses. He is not asking the church to take his word alone.

His strongest point is ‘the same gift’. At Pentecost the Spirit came on Jewish believers. In Caesarea the Spirit came on Gentile believers ‘just as’ he had come on them. If God has made no difference, the church cannot make one.

‘Repentance’ means a change of mind that turns the whole life around, away from sin and toward God. The believers say God has ‘granted’ it. It is God's gift, not something the Gentiles earned by first becoming Jews. ‘Unto life’ means it leads to life with God, now and in the age to come.

The church in Jerusalem does something hard here. It changes its mind when it sees what God has done. Their silence and their praise go together.

The angel's words, ‘a message by which you and all your household will be saved’, show why Cornelius needed Peter. His prayers had been heard, and the answer was the good news about Jesus.
passages.ot:
The Lord's words that Peter remembers go back to John the Baptist and to Jesus himself: “For John baptized with water, but in a few days you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 1:5). John's own preaching stood on the prophets' promise that God would pour out his Spirit.

‘Repentance unto life’ echoes the prophets' call. God says through Ezekiel, “For I take no pleasure in anyone’s death, declares the Lord GOD. So repent and live!” (Ezekiel 18:32). What God once called Israel to, he now gives to the nations as well.

And the Psalms had prayed for exactly this: “that Your ways may be known on earth, Your salvation among all nations” (Psalm 67:2).
passages.asks: ‘Who was I to hinder the work of God?’ Ask whether there is anyone you have, in your heart, kept at a distance from God's welcome. The believers in Jerusalem let the evidence change them, and then they praised God for it. Changing your mind for God's sake is not weakness. It is worship.

passages.happening:
Luke goes back to the believers scattered by the persecution after Stephen's death. They travel as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, “speaking the message only to Jews” (verse 19). But some of them, men from Cyprus and Cyrene, come to Antioch and begin speaking to the Greeks as well, telling the good news about the Lord Jesus (verse 20). “The hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number of people believed and turned to the Lord” (verse 21).

The church in Jerusalem hears of it and sends Barnabas to Antioch. When he arrives and sees the grace of God, he rejoices and encourages them all to stay true to the Lord with all their hearts (verses 22-23). “Barnabas was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and faith”, and a great number of people are brought to the Lord (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
Antioch was a great city in Syria, near the modern city of Antakya in southern Turkey. It was founded around 300 BC by Seleucus, one of the generals who divided the empire of Alexander the Great, and in Roman times it was the capital of the province of Syria. It was one of the great cities of the eastern empire. Phoenicia was the coast of Tyre and Sidon. Cyprus is the large island off that coast, Barnabas's home (4:36). Cyrene was a Greek city in North Africa, in what is now Libya.

At first the scattered believers spoke ‘only to Jews’. That was natural: the good news was about Israel's Messiah, and the synagogue was where people knew the Scriptures. Then some unnamed believers took a new step. They spoke to Greeks, people who were not Jews, and many believed. No apostle planned it. Luke does not even record their names. Some of the most important steps in the church's story were taken by people whose names are lost.

They spoke of ‘the Lord Jesus’. To Greek ears, ‘Lord’ was a title given to gods and to the emperor. To call Jesus Lord was to say he stood above them all.

The Jerusalem church sends Barnabas to look. It is a good choice. He was himself from Cyprus, like some of the preachers. And he does not come to inspect or to find fault. He ‘saw the grace of God’ and was glad.
passages.ot:
The prophets had pictured the day when people of the nations would join themselves to Israel's God. Zechariah wrote: “In those days ten men from the nations of every tongue will tightly grasp the robe of a Jew, saying, ‘Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.’” (Zechariah 8:23). In Antioch, Greeks take hold of the message brought by Jews from Cyprus and Cyrene.

‘The hand of the Lord was with them’ is a phrase from the Old Testament for God's power at work, as when Ezra says “the hand of the LORD his God was upon him” (Ezra 7:6).
passages.asks: Barnabas ‘saw the grace of God’ in a new kind of church, and he was glad. Ask what you look for first when you see a church or a believer unlike yourself: what is missing, or where God is at work. And remember the unnamed men from Cyprus and Cyrene. Faithfulness does not need to be famous.

passages.happening: Barnabas goes to Tarsus to look for Saul (verse 25). When he finds him, he brings him back to Antioch. For a whole year they meet with the church and teach large numbers of people. “The disciples were first called Christians at Antioch” (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
Saul had been sent home to Tarsus some time before (9:30). We do not know what he did there. Barnabas remembers him, goes looking, and brings him into the work. Once again Barnabas opens a door for Saul.

For a year they teach. A new church of Jews and Greeks needs to learn the Scriptures, the story of Jesus, and how to live together.

Then comes a famous line: ‘The disciples were first called Christians at Antioch.’ The word means ‘Christ's people’, those who belong to Christ. Its ending was a Latin way of naming the followers of a leader. Gospel writers name a group called the Herodians, the supporters of Herod (Mark 3:6), in the same way.

Who first used the name? Luke does not say. Most scholars think outsiders coined it, perhaps the people of Antioch, because this group was no longer just one more kind of Jew: Greeks were in it too, and Christ was at its centre. Whether it began as a mocking nickname or simply as a label is not known. In the New Testament the name appears only three times: here; on the lips of King Agrippa, “Can you persuade me in such a short time to become a Christian?” (26:28); and in Peter's letter: “if you suffer as a Christian, do not be ashamed” (1 Peter 4:16). The believers' own names for themselves in Acts are ‘disciples’, ‘brothers’, ‘saints’, and followers of ‘the Way’.

‘Christ’ is the Greek word for the Hebrew ‘Messiah’, the anointed king. So the name, even if outsiders gave it, said something true: these were the people of Israel's Messiah, Jews and Greeks together.
passages.ot:
The name points back to the Old Testament hope of the Messiah, the anointed one. Kings in Israel were anointed with oil, and God promised David a son whose kingdom would last forever (2 Samuel 7:16). The Psalms speak of the LORD and “His Anointed One” (Psalm 2:2). The Greek for ‘Anointed One’ is Christos.

Isaiah also promised that God's people would be called by a new name: “Nations will see your righteousness, and all kings your glory. You will be called by a new name that the mouth of the LORD will bestow” (Isaiah 62:2). Christians have often seen a hint of that promise here, though Luke does not say so.
passages.asks: The name ‘Christian’ may have been given by outsiders, who could see what the believers were about: Christ. Ask what people who watch your life would call you. And notice Barnabas going to Tarsus to find Saul. Part of serving God is seeing gifts in others, and making room for them.

passages.t: Agabus, and a gift for Judea
passages.happening:
Prophets come down from Jerusalem to Antioch. One of them, named Agabus, stands up and predicts through the Spirit that “a great famine would sweep across the whole world” (verse 28). Luke adds, “This happened under Claudius.”

So the disciples, each according to his ability, decide to send help to the believers living in Judea (verse 29). They send their gifts to the elders, by the hands of Barnabas and Saul (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
A prophet in the early church was someone who spoke a message from God to the believers, sometimes about what was coming. Agabus appears again much later, when he warns Paul of chains in Jerusalem (21:10-11).

Claudius was the Roman emperor from AD 41 to 54. ‘The whole world’ was a common way of speaking of the lands of the empire. Ancient writers tell of food shortages in several places during his reign. The Jewish historian Josephus describes a severe famine in Judea in the mid-40s, when Queen Helena of Adiabene, a convert to Judaism, bought grain in Egypt and figs in Cyprus for the people of Jerusalem. Most think this is the famine Luke means, though its exact years are uncertain.

Look at what the believers in Antioch do. They hear of a coming hardship, and they act before it arrives. Each gives ‘according to his ability’: no one is told an amount, and no one is left out. A church made largely of Greeks sends help to Jewish believers in Judea, most of whom they have never met. The people who brought them the gospel now receive their care.

‘Elders’ appear here for the first time in the church. In Jewish towns and synagogues, elders were respected older men who led the community, and the church took up the same word. Acts 14 and 15 say more.

This visit of Barnabas and Saul to Jerusalem may be the one Paul describes in Galatians 2:1-10, when the leaders asked him “to remember the poor” (Galatians 2:10). Others think Galatians 2 is the council of Acts 15. The book page's part on Acts and Paul's letters sets out the views and does not settle them.
passages.ot:
The Law commanded open hands: “I am commanding you to open wide your hand to your brother and to the poor and needy in your land” (Deuteronomy 15:11). In Joseph's day, when famine came, God had prepared a store of grain beforehand, and “every nation came to Joseph in Egypt to buy grain, because the famine was severe over all the earth” (Genesis 41:57). Here, warned by a prophet, the church also prepares.

Paul would later explain why Gentile believers gave to Jewish believers in Jerusalem: “if the Gentiles have shared in their spiritual blessings, they are obligated to minister to them with material blessings” (Romans 15:27). The gift from Antioch is the first sign of that.
passages.asks: The believers at Antioch gave before the famine came, each as he was able, to people far away. Ask whether there is someone whose need you can see coming, and whether you could act before it arrives. Generosity across distance, culture and language is one of the clearest signs that a church has understood the gospel.
